**James Damore and the "Ideological Echo Chamber" memo**
In 2017, Google engineer James Damore circulated an internal memo titled "Google's Ideological Echo Chamber." It argued that the gender gap in tech was partly due to biological differences between men and women and that the company's culture silenced conservative views. After the memo leaked in August 2017, Google fired him. The memo cited sources such as John Tierney's City Journal essay "The Real War on Science."

**Timnit Gebru**
The co-leader of Google's Ethical AI team, who studied bias in artificial intelligence. Google pushed her out in December 2020 in a dispute over a research paper criticizing large language models. Her firing caused a major outcry and helped spur the formation of the Alphabet Workers Union in January 2021, a minority union that quickly grew to several hundred members.

**Sundar Pichai and alleged bias against conservatives**
Pichai has been Google's CEO since 2015 and later also became CEO of its parent company Alphabet. In 2018 he testified before the House Judiciary Committee about accusations that Google's search algorithms buried conservative websites, and Google executives faced further questioning by Senate Republicans in 2019.

**Department of Justice search antitrust case**
In 2019 the Justice Department announced an antitrust investigation of Google, and in 2020 it sued the company for illegally maintaining a monopoly over online search, partly by paying companies like Apple to make Google the default search engine. In August 2024 Judge Amit Mehta ruled that Google was an illegal monopolist.

**Ad tech antitrust case**
A second Justice Department lawsuit, filed in 2023 in Virginia, accused Google of monopolizing the technology used to buy and sell online advertising. The government unusually asked for a jury trial, but Google paid the claimed damages in advance so the case was tried by a judge. In 2025 Judge Leonie Brinkema ruled that Google had illegally monopolized parts of the ad tech market.

**Larry Page, Sergey Brin, and the 2004 IPO**
Page and Brin founded Google in 1998 while they were PhD students at Stanford. The company went public in a highly anticipated initial public offering in August 2004, using an unusual Dutch-auction format to sell its shares.

**Alphabet and Waymo**
In 2015 Google reorganized so that Alphabet Inc. became the parent company of Google and its other ventures. One of those ventures is Waymo, which grew out of Google's self-driving car project and runs driverless taxi services in several U.S. cities.

**YouTube and other acquisitions**
Google has bought many companies, most famously the video site YouTube in 2006. Others include DoubleClick (online advertising), Keyhole (whose technology became Google Earth), GrandCentral (which became Google Voice), and the question-answering service Aardvark. Older Google services include the social network Orkut, the photo program Picasa, and the blogging platform Blogger.

**Sycamore and Willow quantum chips**
In 2019 Google claimed its 53-qubit Sycamore processor had achieved "quantum supremacy" by completing a calculation that would take a classical supercomputer thousands of years. In December 2024 it announced the 105-qubit Willow chip, which showed improved quantum error correction. Google's quantum hardware was later used to simulate a Floquet system, a quantum system driven periodically in time.

**Google v. Oracle**
A long legal fight over whether Google infringed Oracle's copyright by copying parts of the Java programming interface (API) when building the Android operating system. In 2021 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled for Google, holding that its use was fair use.

**Project Maven**
A Pentagon program that used artificial intelligence to analyze video from military drones. After thousands of Google employees protested and some resigned, Google decided in 2018 not to renew its contract for the project.

**2018 Google Walkout and Andy Rubin**
In November 2018, about 20,000 Google employees around the world walked out to protest how the company handled sexual harassment. The protest followed reports that Android creator Andy Rubin had received a roughly $90 million exit package despite a misconduct allegation against him.

**Margrethe Vestager and the EU fine**
Vestager, the European Union's competition commissioner, fined Google €2.42 billion (about $2.7 billion) in June 2017 for abusing its dominance by favoring its own Google Shopping service in search results. The EU later fined Google even larger amounts in cases involving Android and online advertising.

**Gemini and AI Overviews (Penske Media lawsuit)**
Gemini is Google's family of AI models, which powers the AI Overviews that summarize answers at the top of search results. In 2025 Penske Media, the publisher of Rolling Stone, Billboard, and Variety, sued Google, arguing that these AI summaries use publishers' content and take away their web traffic.

**"Don't be evil" and 20 percent time**
"Don't be evil" was Google's famous unofficial motto, coined by early employees. The company also became known for "20 percent time" (Innovation Time Off), a policy encouraging engineers to spend about a fifth of their time on side projects, which helped produce products like Gmail.
